newsitem.title: CHINA: Australia's Howard raises rights issue with China.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard raises rights issue with China.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Monday assured Chinese Premier Li Peng that Canberra wanted close ties with Beijing but warned that disagreements over human rights could arise in future.
Howard also appealed to the Chinese leader to release jailed Australian businessman James Peng and said such a move would help relations between the two countries.

"I said inevitably in the area of human rights there would be differences," Howard told a news conference after his meeting. "I don't think it's realistic to imagine that human rights issues are not going to crop up.
"I raised specifically the issue of James Peng. I said the Chinese government should release him on compassionate grounds."

Peng was jailed for 18 years in September 1995 after being convicted of embezzling about $180,000 in a case linked to his publicly listed company Champaign Industrial, based in the south China city of Shenzhen.
His family has said he was abducted in the Portuguese enclave of Macau and bundled across the border into China where he was handed over to authorities.
Peng has insisted the charges were a trumped up effort by powerful business rivals to gain hold of his company.
"I said it was a matter that should be resolved because Peng is an Australian resident and it would have beneficial effects," Howard said without elaborating.
Li replied the case was a matter for the courts but he would relay Australian concerns.
Howard has said the main aim of his visit was to boost commercial ties.
"I want to assure you that Australia is committed to a very close bilateral relationship," he told the Chinese premier.
Howard arrived in the Chinese capital on Sunday from Shanghai, where he hailed China's economic boom as presenting Australian firms with huge opportunities.
China is Australia's fifth largest trading partner, with two-way trade worth $6.3 billion in the year to June 30, 1996.

Travelling with the prime minister is a business group that includes representatives of firms that already have a strong presence in the Chinese market as well as companies looking to tap into new areas such as finance.

Howard's visit is also intended to help repair damage to relations from issues including Canberra's military ties with the United States and its hosting last year of exiled Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama.
